html:
A standard rain gauge used in Korea under the Joseon dynasty, introduced in 1441 under Sejong the Great.

It was a simple iron or bronze cylinder on a stone stand. Officials measured the depth of water after each rain with a ruler and reported it to the capital. Gauges of the same size were sent to every provincial office, so that readings from across the country could be compared. This is the main reason it is often called the first network of rain gauges.

The point was farming and tax. Rice needs water at the right time, and the state set its grain tax by the harvest, so it wanted to know how much rain each region received. Sejong's court also produced water clocks, sundials and a new calendar, and the Hangul alphabet. Rain records from the later Joseon period survive for Seoul from 1777 on. Only one old cheugugi remains, from 1837, now a national treasure.
sum: A standard rain gauge used in Korea under the Joseon dynasty, introduced in 1441 under Sejong the Great.
